role.altitude: The train driver keeps talking with traffic control, inspecting the locomotive, checking brakes and calling out signals; writing down instructions, reading paper defect books and brake sheets and filling paper checklists shrink.
skills_to_grow: Using the cab tablet for checklists, defect lists and brake data
role.ambitious_version: A driver who starts each run with defects, brake data and written instructions on one screen and spends the time on the walk-round.

tasks.short: Receive information from traffic control by radiophone on stops, delays or oncoming trains, repeat it back, confer with the conductor, and note written instructions.

steps.what: Train driver receives information from traffic control by radiophone on stops, delays or oncoming trains
Train driver repeats the message back and confirms it
Train driver confers with the conductor by radiophone on stops and delays
Train driver takes down written instructions from traffic control: by hand today; after the change, for instructions sent as text, reads them on the cab tablet
Train driver checks the text instruction against the radio message: location, speed and limits say the same
Train driver confirms the checked instruction on the cab tablet

tasks.design: Spoken radio communication with repeat-back stays exactly as it is. Where traffic control already issues written instructions as text, they appear on the cab tablet and the driver confirms them after the radio repeat-back, instead of writing them down by hand while stopped.

approvals.approved_version: The confirmation of the written instruction exactly as checked by the driver in s4c against the radio message, sent once to traffic control; a changed instruction needs a new check and confirmation.

tasks.previous_blocker: Written instructions were copied by hand from the radio.
tasks.enabler_now: Text instructions from traffic control on cab tablets.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing that a controller is unsure and asking again.

evidence.claim: Traffic control can send written instructions as text to cab tablets.
AI as a rail safety component falls under the rail interoperability rules; this design adds no AI to train control.

assumptions: Boundary: radio communication; interpreting train orders and rules (task 12752) is a sibling task.
Input contract for s4: traffic control's system sends written instructions as text, for about half of instructions; s4 is priced at that share.
Radio talk, repeat-back, the check and the confirmation keep their full time. About half of written instructions come as text, so s4 keeps 55.
unknowns: Share of instructions issued as text.
research_questions: Do errors in written instructions fall?

incremental.description: No ongoing new work: writing instructions by hand where data coverage fails is inside s4, and learning the confirmation is a one-off.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: poor data coverage means only about a quarter of instructions arrive as text, so s4 keeps 80 (2.6); high: half of instructions arrive as text as assumed (5.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Inspect locomotives for mechanical problems, verify adequate fuel, sand and water, read known defects, and record the check and report defects before each run.

steps.what: Train driver inspects the locomotive for mechanical problems on the walk-round
Train driver verifies adequate fuel, sand and water
Train driver reads known defects for the locomotive
Train driver records the pre-run check: on a paper checklist today; ticked on the tablet after the change, with locomotive and time filled in
Train driver writes up each new defect for maintenance: by phone today; in the tablet's defect form after the change
Train driver takes a photo of the defect
Train driver checks the defect report before sending: the defect described matches what was found, with the right locomotive and photo
Train driver sends the checked defect report to the maintenance depot

tasks.design: The walk-round stays hands-on. Fuel and water levels are read from the cab display where the locomotive has sensors; sand is still checked by eye. Known defects come from the maintenance system onto the cab tablet instead of a paper defect book. The pre-run checklist is ticked on the tablet. For a new defect the driver writes it up in the tablet's defect form, takes a photo, checks the report and sends it to the maintenance depot instead of phoning. Checklist records show who checked what; any use beyond safety records is agreed with the works council first.

approvals.approved_version: The defect report with locomotive, description and photo exactly as checked by the driver in s4c, sent once to the maintenance depot's system; any change needs a new check.

tasks.enabler_now: Cab tablets linked to the maintenance system and onboard level sensors.

reach.learn: Whether defects arrive earlier and with photos.

evidence.claim: Cab tablets can show defect lists from maintenance systems and take checklists.
Cab apps that can be used to watch drivers' behaviour or performance need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: pre-run inspection; reports on accidents, signal problems and delays (task 12760) and cab documentation (task 12761) are sibling tasks.
Input contract for s2: level sensors on about half of the locomotive fleet; s2 is priced at that share.
Input contract for s3: defects entered by the depot in the maintenance system.
The walk-round keeps its full time.

Sizing: ticking the checklist on the tablet takes about as long as on paper, so s4 keeps 90 for the filled-in locomotive and time only. s3 keeps 80 because defects for this locomotive are listed in one place. Writing a defect up keeps 70 because the phone call goes; the photo, the check and the send keep their full time.
unknowns: Share of locomotives with level sensors.
research_questions: Are defects repaired before the next run more often?

incremental.description: Train driver reports checklist items that do not fit the locomotive type.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few locomotives get level sensors (s2 keeps 85) and the depot enters defects late (s3 keeps 90) (6.2); high: sensors on half the fleet and defects kept current as assumed (10.2).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Confirm with shunting staff that the brake examination test was conducted, check the brake data against the route's requirement, observe the brake test from the cab, and record it.

steps.what: Train driver confirms with shunting staff or the carriage inspector that the brake examination test was conducted
Train driver checks the brake sheet: train composition and brake percentage against the route's requirement
Train driver observes brake pipe pressure during the brake test from the cab
Train driver records the brake test: on paper today; on the tablet checklist after the change, with the time stamp filled in

tasks.design: Train composition and brake data come from the operator's train composition system onto the cab tablet, which computes the brake percentage and shows whether it meets the route's requirement, instead of the driver adding up a paper brake sheet. The driver still confirms the test with shunting staff and watches the brake pipe pressure. The test is recorded on the tablet checklist with a time stamp.
tasks.previous_blocker: Brake sheets were filled and added up on paper.
tasks.enabler_now: Train composition data on cab tablets.
tasks.still_hard: Wagons whose brake data are missing from the system.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing that a brake pipe pressure falls too slowly.

reach.learn: Whether brake data mismatches are caught at the yard.

evidence.claim: Train composition systems can supply brake data to cab tablets.
A report or checklist tool is not an AI safety component under the rail rules.

assumptions: Boundary: checking brake tests; monitoring brake air pressure while driving (task 12750) is a sibling task.
Input contract for s2: wagon brake data kept in the composition system by the operator, for about 80% of trains; s2 is priced at that share.
Confirming and observing keep their full time. s4 keeps 85 because recording the result on the tablet takes about as long as on paper and only the time stamp fills in.

incremental.description: Train driver reports wagons with missing brake data.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many wagons have missing brake data, so about half of the trains still need the paper sheet and s2 keeps 75 (9.4); high: 80% of trains have complete data as assumed (16.9).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Observe each signal, call out train signals to assistants, and verify meanings together.

steps.what: Train driver observes the train signals ahead
Train driver calls out the signal aspect to the assistant
Train driver and assistant verify the signal meaning together

tasks.design: Nothing changes. Calling out and verifying signals is a safety practice done by people in the cab, and no software takes part in it.
tasks.previous_blocker: Nothing blocked it; this is a safety practice.
tasks.still_hard: Signals seen in low sun or fog.
tasks.human_edge: Catching a misread aspect between two people.

evidence.claim: AI as a rail safety component falls under the rail interoperability rules, so no software is added here.

assumptions: Boundary: calling out signals; interpreting signals and rules (task 12752) is a sibling task.
All steps keep their full time.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Nothing changes: observing, calling out and verifying signals is a safety practice done by people in the cab (0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional
